To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a single amino acid deletion in a hybrid sequence peptide results in an endothelin-like structure.

the deletion of one residue of an apamin-related peptide sequence results in a change from a beta-turn to an alpha-helix, with the formation of a different disulfide crosslink pattern than that of apamin.
deletion of one residue in an apamin sequence changes its folding to that of endothelium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural characterization of a peptide sequence that contains a single deletion of a single residue.
the folding of a hybrid sequence related to the bee-venom peptide apamin.
the relationship between the structure and biological activity of peptides, particularly those containing disulfide cross-links.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the deletion of the K4 residue in the apamin scaffold region results in the formation of a new disulfide pattern that is analogous to that observed in endothelin, but the AD peptide is still more similar in structure to the helical apamin than to endothelin.
the solution structure of a peptide can depend upon its sequence.
the deletion of the single amino acid K4 of the N-terminal scaffold of apamin results in an alpha-helically folded peptide, with the disulfide arrangement analogous to that of endothelins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a change of only one amino acid in the apamin scaffold region is sufficient to change the folding of the peptide from the helical apamin to the helical endothelin.
a change of one amino acid in the scaffold region of the apamil sequence results in an alpha-helically folded peptide, which has the same disulfide cross link pattern as endothelin.

a single amino acid deletion in an apamin scaffold peptide results in a helix, with a disulfide pairing that is similar to that of endothelins, and that the helix is stabilized in a manner analogous to that of endothelial helices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single residue change in the scaffold region can change the folding of a peptide to that of an unrelated peptide.
a small deletion of a single amino-acid can have a profound effect on peptide folding.
a single amino acid deletion can change the folding of an entire peptide.
